segments.text: Welcome to Application of Integrals. You already know the area of a rectangle, a triangle, or a circle from memorised formulas. But what is the area of a region trapped under a curvy boundary, like under the arch y equals x squared plus one? There is no clean formula — and integration is exactly what fills that gap.

Here is the picture to carry through the whole chapter. Imagine a land surveyor measuring an irregular farm plot. One edge runs along a straight canal — that's our x-axis — and the opposite edge is a wavy stream described by some curve y equals f of x.
The clever surveyor slices the plot into a long series of very thin vertical strips, each as narrow as a sheet of paper.
Each strip is almost a rectangle: its width is a tiny d x, and its height is the value of the curve at that spot, so one strip has area about y d x, which is f of x d x.

<curious> To get the whole plot, add up the areas of all these strips from the well at x equals a to the banyan tree at x equals b. Adding up infinitely many infinitely-thin strips is precisely what the definite integral means: the area is the integral from a to b of f of x d x.

Sometimes the boundary is measured more naturally against the vertical canal — the curve is given as x equals g of y. Then the same logic just flips axes, and you sweep horizontal strips up the y-axis.
In that case each strip is horizontal, with height d y and length x equals g of y, swept from y equals c to y equals d.

The one habit to install now: pick the variable that matches the geometry. If the region is walled left and right by vertical lines, d x strips win; if it's capped above and below by horizontal lines, d y strips are cleaner. Choose badly and a one-line integral becomes a messy two-piece one.

Application of Integrals में स्वागत है। rectangle, triangle, या circle की area तुम memorised formulas से जानते हो। पर किसी curvy boundary के नीचे फँसे region की area क्या है, जैसे arch y equals x squared plus one के नीचे? कोई clean formula नहीं है — और integration ठीक वही gap भरता है।

यह picture पूरे chapter में साथ ले जाओ। एक land surveyor सोचो जो एक irregular farm plot माप रहा है। एक edge एक straight canal के साथ चलती है — वो हमारा x-axis है — और opposite edge एक wavy stream है जिसे किसी curve y equals f of x से describe किया गया है।
clever surveyor plot को बहुत पतली vertical strips की एक लंबी series में slice करता है, हर एक कागज़ की शीट जितनी पतली।
हर strip लगभग एक rectangle है: उसकी width एक tiny d x है, और height उस जगह curve की value है, तो एक strip की area लगभग y d x है, यानी f of x d x।

<curious> पूरा plot पाने के लिए, इन सारी strips की areas को well पर x equals a से banyan tree पर x equals b तक add करो। infinitely many infinitely-thin strips को add करना ही exactly वो है जो definite integral का मतलब है: area है integral from a to b of f of x d x।

कभी-कभी boundary vertical canal के against ज़्यादा naturally मापी जाती है — curve x equals g of y के रूप में दिया होता है। तब वही logic बस axes flip कर देता है, और तुम horizontal strips को y-axis पर sweep करते हो।
उस case में हर strip horizontal है, height d y और length x equals g of y के साथ, y equals c से y equals d तक swept।

अभी डालने वाली एक habit: वो variable चुनो जो geometry से match करे। अगर region vertical lines से left और right walled हो, तो d x strips जीतती हैं; अगर horizontal lines से ऊपर-नीचे capped हो, तो d y strips cleaner हैं। गलत चुनो और एक one-line integral एक messy two-piece बन जाता है।

sections.title: Area as the limit of a sum

board_events.text: Why the strip formula is exactly the definite integral
Take $f$ continuous and non-negative on $[a,b]$.

board_events.latex: \Delta x = \frac{b-a}{n}, \quad a = x_0 < x_1 < \cdots < x_n = b

board_events.text: The $i$-th strip is a rectangle of height $f(\xi_i)$ and width $\Delta x$.
Thinner strips ⇒ smaller error slivers between rectangle and true curve.
The final equality is the definition of the definite integral (a Riemann sum).

segments.text: Let's make the strip picture rigorous — this is the theorem that justifies the whole method. Take f continuous and non-negative on the interval from a to b.
Partition that interval into n sub-intervals, each of width delta x equal to b minus a over n, with division points from x-nought up to x-n.
The width of each piece is delta x, and the division points march evenly across the interval.
Over the i-th sub-interval, pick any sample point xi-sub-i. The thin strip standing there is approximately a rectangle of height f of xi-sub-i and width delta x.
Summing all these rectangles gives an approximation to the area: S-n equals the sum over i of f of xi-sub-i times delta x.

<curious> Now here's why it becomes exact. The thinner the strips, the smaller the sliver of error between each rectangle and the true curved strip. As we let n go to infinity, so delta x shrinks to zero, those slivers vanish completely.
So the approximating sum converges to the exact area: the limit as n goes to infinity of that sum equals the integral from a to b of f of x d x.
And that final equality is not a coincidence — it is the very definition of the definite integral as a Riemann sum. The strip intuition and the integral are one and the same thing.
चलो strip picture को rigorous बनाएँ — यही वो theorem है जो पूरी method justify करता है। f को interval a से b पर continuous और non-negative लो।
उस interval को n sub-intervals में partition करो, हर एक की width delta x equal to b minus a over n, division points x-nought से x-n तक।
हर piece की width delta x है, और division points interval पर evenly चलते हैं।
i-th sub-interval पर, कोई भी sample point xi-sub-i चुनो। वहाँ खड़ी thin strip लगभग एक rectangle है height f of xi-sub-i और width delta x के साथ।
इन सारी rectangles को sum करने पर area का एक approximation मिलता है: S-n equals sum over i of f of xi-sub-i times delta x।

<curious> अब यह exact क्यों बनता है। strips जितनी पतली, हर rectangle और true curved strip के बीच error का sliver उतना छोटा। जैसे ही हम n को infinity तक ले जाते हैं, तो delta x zero तक सिकुड़ता है, वो slivers पूरी तरह गायब हो जाते हैं।
तो approximating sum exact area तक converge करता है: n के infinity जाने पर उस sum की limit equals integral from a to b of f of x d x।
और वो final equality कोई coincidence नहीं — यह definite integral की एक Riemann sum के रूप में परिभाषा ही है। strip intuition और integral एक ही चीज़ हैं।

board_events.text: For the ellipse, the upper half is $y = \tfrac{b}{a}\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}$.
Degeneration check: set $b = a$ and $\pi ab$ collapses to $\pi a^2$ — the circle.
Symmetry is the time-saver: compute one symmetric part, then multiply.

segments.text: Now two results worth memorising — the areas of a circle and an ellipse — both proved the same clean way, using symmetry plus one standard antiderivative.

That antiderivative is the workhorse of the whole chapter: the integral of root a squared minus x squared is x over two times root a squared minus x squared, plus a squared over two times inverse sine of x over a, plus a constant.

For the circle x squared plus y squared equals a squared, exploit symmetry about both axes. The total area is four times the first-quadrant area, where the upper boundary is y equals root a squared minus x squared and x runs from zero to a.

<curious> Evaluating that standard integral from zero to a gives pi a squared over four, so four times it is exactly pi a squared. Integrating only the first quadrant removes any sign ambiguity and lets us evaluate the integral just once.
The ellipse follows immediately. Solving its equation for the upper half gives y equals b over a, times root a squared minus x squared.
By the same two-axis symmetry, the area is four b over a times the same integral from zero to a — which we already know is pi a squared over four — so the ellipse area is pi a b.

<whisper> And here is a beautiful self-check. Set b equal to a, and the ellipse collapses into a circle — and its area pi a b collapses correctly into pi a squared. A formula that degenerates correctly is almost certainly right.

The lesson under both proofs is symmetry: whenever a region is symmetric about an axis, compute the area of one symmetric part and simply multiply. It is the single biggest time-saver in this chapter.
अब दो memorise करने लायक results — circle और ellipse की areas — दोनों एक ही clean तरीके से prove किए गए, symmetry plus एक standard antiderivative से।

वो antiderivative पूरे chapter का workhorse है: integral of root a squared minus x squared है x over two times root a squared minus x squared, plus a squared over two times inverse sine of x over a, plus एक constant।

circle x squared plus y squared equals a squared के लिए, दोनों axes के बारे में symmetry का फ़ायदा उठाओ। total area first-quadrant area का four times है, जहाँ upper boundary y equals root a squared minus x squared है और x zero से a तक चलता है।

<curious> उस standard integral को zero से a तक evaluate करने पर pi a squared over four मिलता है, तो उसका four times exactly pi a squared है। सिर्फ़ first quadrant integrate करना कोई भी sign ambiguity हटा देता है और integral को एक ही बार evaluate करने देता है।
ellipse तुरंत follow करता है। इसके equation को upper half के लिए solve करने पर y equals b over a, times root a squared minus x squared मिलता है।
उसी two-axis symmetry से, area है four b over a times वही integral zero से a तक — जो हम पहले से जानते हैं pi a squared over four है — तो ellipse area है pi a b।

<whisper> और यह रहा एक खूबसूरत self-check। b को a के बराबर रखो, और ellipse एक circle में collapse हो जाता है — और उसकी area pi a b सही तरीके से pi a squared में collapse होती है। जो formula सही degenerate होता है वो लगभग निश्चित रूप से सही है।
दोनों proofs के नीचे का सबक symmetry है: जब भी कोई region किसी axis के बारे में symmetric हो, एक symmetric part की area निकालो और बस multiply करो। यह इस chapter का सबसे बड़ा time-saver है।

sections.title: The area formulas and the standard catalogue

board_events.text: All the Subtopic-1 formulas in one place
The plain integral is SIGNED; area is never negative. Below/crossing the axis, use $|f|$.

segments.text: Let's consolidate every formula from this subtopic in one place. Keep them together — they are variations on a single idea.
For a curve above the x-axis, the area is the integral from a to b of y d x, which is the integral of f of x d x.
For a curve measured against the y-axis, with x a function of y, the area is the integral from c to d of x d y.
When the curve lies entirely below the x-axis, the raw integral comes out negative, so the area is its absolute value, equal to minus the integral.
And when the curve crosses the axis inside the interval, the honest area is the integral of the absolute value of f — you split at the crossing and add the magnitudes.
Two catalogue results worth memorising for speed: the circle of radius a has area pi a squared, and the ellipse with semi-axes a and b has area pi a b.
And the workhorse antiderivative once more: the integral of root a squared minus x squared, which you will reach for in every circle and ellipse problem.

<whisper> The one warning that governs this entire subtopic: the plain definite integral is a signed number, but area is never negative. Below or across the axis, you must switch to the absolute value of f and split at every root.
चलो इस subtopic का हर formula एक जगह consolidate करें। इन्हें साथ रखो — ये एक ही idea के variations हैं।
x-axis के ऊपर वाले curve के लिए, area है integral from a to b of y d x, यानी integral of f of x d x।
y-axis के against मापे गए curve के लिए, जहाँ x, y का function है, area है integral from c to d of x d y।
जब curve पूरी तरह x-axis के नीचे हो, raw integral negative आता है, तो area उसकी absolute value है, minus the integral के बराबर।
और जब curve interval के अंदर axis को cross करे, honest area है f की absolute value का integral — तुम crossing पर split करते हो और magnitudes जोड़ते हो।
speed के लिए दो memorise करने लायक catalogue results: radius a के circle की area pi a squared है, और semi-axes a और b वाले ellipse की area pi a b।
और एक बार फिर workhorse antiderivative: integral of root a squared minus x squared, जिसे तुम हर circle और ellipse problem में reach करोगे।

<whisper> एक warning जो पूरे इस subtopic को चलाती है: plain definite integral एक signed number है, पर area कभी negative नहीं। axis के नीचे या across, तुम्हें f की absolute value पर switch करना होगा और हर root पर split करना होगा।

sections.title: A clean area above the axis

board_events.text: Area bounded by y = x² + 2, the x-axis, x = 0 and x = 2
Since $x^2 + 2 > 0$ everywhere, the curve lies entirely above the axis — no sign worries.
Whenever $f(x) > 0$ across the whole interval, just integrate directly.

segments.text: Let's start with a clean board-level example. We want the area bounded by the curve y equals x squared plus two, the x-axis, and the vertical lines x equals zero and x equals two.
First, the safety check. Since x squared plus two is always positive, the curve lies entirely above the x-axis, so there are no sign worries and we can integrate straight through.
So the area is simply the integral from zero to two of x squared plus two d x.
Antidifferentiate term by term: x squared integrates to x cubed over three, and two integrates to two x.
Now evaluate at the limits. At x equals two we get eight thirds plus four; at x equals zero everything vanishes. So the value is eight thirds plus four, which is eight plus twelve over three.
That gives twenty over three. So the area is twenty over three square units.
The takeaway is simple: whenever the function stays positive across the whole interval, there is no absolute value and no splitting — you just integrate directly.
चलो एक clean board-level example से शुरू करें। हमें curve y equals x squared plus two, x-axis, और vertical lines x equals zero और x equals two से bounded area चाहिए।
पहले, safety check। चूँकि x squared plus two हमेशा positive है, curve पूरी तरह x-axis के ऊपर है, तो कोई sign worries नहीं और हम सीधे integrate कर सकते हैं।
तो area बस है integral from zero to two of x squared plus two d x।
term by term antidifferentiate करो: x squared integrate होकर x cubed over three बनता है, और two integrate होकर two x।
अब limits पर evaluate करो। x equals two पर हमें eight thirds plus four मिलता है; x equals zero पर सब कुछ गायब हो जाता है। तो value है eight thirds plus four, यानी eight plus twelve over three।
इससे मिलता है twenty over three। तो area है twenty over three square units।
takeaway simple है: जब भी function पूरे interval पर positive रहे, कोई absolute value नहीं और कोई splitting नहीं — तुम बस सीधे integrate करते हो।

board_events.text: The trap: $\int_{-2}^{2} x^3\,dx = 0$ because $x^3$ is odd — but the region is not empty!
Fix: area is $\int |f|\,dx$. Split at the crossing $x = 0$ and use symmetry.
The instant a curve changes sign on the interval — stop and split.

segments.text: This example is a classic speed trap, and it teaches the single most important rule of the subtopic. We want the area bounded by y equals x cubed and the x-axis, from x equals minus two to x equals two.
Look at the picture. The cubic dips below the axis on the left half and rises above it on the right half, crossing at the origin.

<whisper> Here is the trap. A hurried student writes the integral from minus two to two of x cubed. Because x cubed is an odd function, that integral equals zero — and they tick zero. But the region is plainly not empty; the two signed pieces have simply cancelled.
The fix is to compute the area as the integral of the absolute value of f. Split at the crossing point x equals zero, and use symmetry, since the two halves have equal area.
So the area is the magnitude of the integral from minus two to zero, plus the integral from zero to two — which, by symmetry, is just twice the integral from zero to two of x cubed.
Evaluating, x cubed integrates to x to the fourth over four, giving twice sixteen over four.
That comes to eight. So the true area is eight square units, not zero.
Burn in the mental shortcut: the instant you see a curve that changes sign on the interval, stop and split. Never integrate straight across a root.
यह example एक classic speed trap है, और यह इस subtopic का सबसे ज़रूरी rule सिखाता है। हमें y equals x cubed और x-axis से bounded area चाहिए, x equals minus two से x equals two तक।
picture देखो। cubic left half पर axis के नीचे झुकता है और right half पर ऊपर उठता है, origin पर cross करते हुए।

<whisper> यह रहा trap। एक जल्दबाज़ student integral from minus two to two of x cubed लिखता है। चूँकि x cubed एक odd function है, वो integral zero के बराबर है — और वो zero tick कर देता है। पर region साफ़ तौर पर empty नहीं है; दोनों signed pieces बस cancel हो गए हैं।
fix है area को f की absolute value के integral के रूप में compute करना। crossing point x equals zero पर split करो, और symmetry use करो, क्योंकि दोनों halves की area बराबर है।
तो area है integral from minus two to zero की magnitude, plus integral from zero to two — जो, symmetry से, बस twice the integral from zero to two of x cubed है।
evaluate करने पर, x cubed integrate होकर x to the fourth over four बनता है, देता है twice sixteen over four।
यह eight आता है। तो true area है eight square units, zero नहीं।
mental shortcut दिमाग में बिठा लो: जैसे ही तुम interval पर sign बदलता curve देखो, रुको और split करो। कभी किसी root के across सीधे integrate मत करो।

sections.title: First-quadrant area under a parabola

board_events.text: First-quadrant area bounded by y² = 4x, the x-axis, and x = 4
The upper branch is $y = 2\sqrt{x}$; the region runs from $x = 0$ to $x = 4$.
Read the boundaries: the $x$-axis being stated means we take ONE branch.
Both branches (no axis stated) would double this to $\tfrac{64}{3}$ by symmetry.

segments.text: This J E E Main level example rewards reading the boundaries carefully. We want the first-quadrant area bounded by the parabola y squared equals four x, the x-axis, and the line x equals four.
From y squared equals four x, the upper branch is y equals two root x. The region sits between the x-axis and this branch, from x equals zero to x equals four.
So the area is the integral from zero to four of two root x d x, which we write as two times the integral of x to the one half.
Antidifferentiating, x to the one half becomes two thirds x to the three halves, so we get four thirds times four to the three halves.
Since four to the three halves is eight, the area is four thirds times eight, which is thirty-two over three square units.

<curious> Now the concept the examiner is really testing — read whether the x-axis is a stated boundary. Because it is stated, the region is bounded below by the axis, so we take only the upper branch.

Had the question asked for the region bounded by the parabola and the line x equals four alone, both branches would be in play, and symmetry would double the answer to sixty-four over three. That one word — axis — decides one branch or two.
यह J E E Main level example boundaries को ध्यान से पढ़ने का इनाम देता है। हमें parabola y squared equals four x, x-axis, और line x equals four से bounded first-quadrant area चाहिए।
y squared equals four x से, upper branch है y equals two root x। region x-axis और इस branch के बीच बैठता है, x equals zero से x equals four तक।
तो area है integral from zero to four of two root x d x, जिसे हम two times the integral of x to the one half लिखते हैं।
antidifferentiate करने पर, x to the one half बनता है two thirds x to the three halves, तो हमें four thirds times four to the three halves मिलता है।
चूँकि four to the three halves है eight, area है four thirds times eight, यानी thirty-two over three square units।
<curious> अब वो concept जो examiner असल में test कर रहा है — पढ़ो कि x-axis एक stated boundary है या नहीं। चूँकि यह stated है, region नीचे से axis से bounded है, तो हम सिर्फ़ upper branch लेते हैं।

अगर question सिर्फ़ parabola और line x equals four से bounded region माँगता, तो दोनों branches खेल में होते, और symmetry answer को sixty-four over three पर double कर देती। वो एक शब्द — axis — तय करता है एक branch या दो।

segments.text: This J E E Advanced example brings the antiderivative and symmetry together. We want the smaller region of the circle x squared plus y squared equals sixteen lying to the right of the line x equals two.
The circle has radius four. The line x equals two is a vertical chord, and the smaller region is the cap between x equals two and x equals four.
This cap is symmetric about the x-axis, so we take the upper half, where y is root sixteen minus x squared, and double it.

So the area is twice the integral from two to four of root sixteen minus x squared. Applying the catalogue antiderivative with a equals four gives x over two, root sixteen minus x squared, plus eight inverse sine of x over four.
Evaluate at the limits. At x equals four, the first term vanishes and inverse sine of one is pi over two, giving four pi. At x equals two, we get two root three plus four pi over three.
Subtracting and doubling: two times the quantity four pi minus two root three plus four pi over three, which simplifies to sixteen pi over three minus four root three.

<curious> Always finish with a sanity check. That value is about nine point eight three, while the full disc is sixteen pi, roughly fifty point three. A cap cut near one-half the radius taking around a fifth of the disc is geometrically reasonable.
यह J E E Advanced example antiderivative और symmetry को साथ लाता है। हमें circle x squared plus y squared equals sixteen का वो smaller region चाहिए जो line x equals two के दाईं ओर है।
circle की radius four है। line x equals two एक vertical chord है, और smaller region x equals two और x equals four के बीच का cap है।
यह cap x-axis के बारे में symmetric है, तो हम upper half लेते हैं, जहाँ y है root sixteen minus x squared, और उसे double करते हैं।

तो area है twice the integral from two to four of root sixteen minus x squared। catalogue antiderivative को a equals four के साथ apply करने पर मिलता है x over two, root sixteen minus x squared, plus eight inverse sine of x over four।
limits पर evaluate करो। x equals four पर, पहला term गायब होता है और inverse sine of one है pi over two, देता है four pi। x equals two पर, हमें two root three plus four pi over three मिलता है।
subtract करके double करो: two times the quantity four pi minus two root three plus four pi over three, जो simplify होकर sixteen pi over three minus four root three बनता है।

<curious> हमेशा एक sanity check से finish करो। वो value लगभग nine point eight three है, जबकि full disc sixteen pi है, करीब fifty point three। radius के लगभग आधे पर कटा cap जो disc का करीब पाँचवाँ हिस्सा लेता है, geometrically reasonable है।

sections.title: Area under curves: the SLiCE reflex

board_events.text: Subtopic 1 — the traps, and the SLiCE routine
AOI-AREA-SIGN: never report a negative or zero 'area' — sketch first, use $\int|f|$.
AOI-AXIS-VAR: a region walled by the $y$-axis wants $\int x\,dy$, not $\int y\,dx$.
AOI-LIMIT-INTERSECT: limits are boundary lines or roots — e.g. $4 - x^2 = 0$ gives $x = \pm 2$.
AOI-SYMM-MISS: after using symmetry, remember to multiply back (× 4 for a circle).
AOI-ELLIPSE-FORM: it is $\pi ab$ — not $\pi a^2 b^2$, not $\pi(a+b)$.
Pro-tip: sketch → mark the roots → check symmetry, all before you integrate.
Mnemonic SLiCE: Sketch → Limits (and roots) → Choose variable → Evaluate (with |·| and symmetry).

segments.text: Let's close the first subtopic with the traps that lose marks and the reflex that prevents them.

The number-one trap is reporting a negative or zero area. Whenever the curve dips below the axis the raw integral goes negative, and if it crosses the axis the pieces cancel. Always sketch first and use the integral of the absolute value of f, splitting at every root.
Second, integrating with respect to the wrong variable. A region walled by the y-axis and horizontal lines wants the integral of x d y, not y d x. Forcing d x there creates needless casework.

Third, inventing the limits. The limits are the boundary lines or the points where the curve meets the axis — not arbitrary numbers. For a curve like four minus x squared bounded by the x-axis, the limits are the roots x equals plus and minus two, which you must solve for.
Fourth, forgetting to multiply back after using symmetry. Computing the first-quadrant area of a circle and then dropping the times-four gives only a quarter of the answer.
Fifth, mangling the ellipse formula. It is pi a b, the product of the semi-axes — not pi a squared b squared, and not pi times a plus b.

<curious> The pro-tip that kills the three biggest mark-losers: before touching the integral, take five seconds to sketch the curve and shade the region, mark where it crosses the axis so you can plan to split, and check for symmetry so you integrate the smallest piece.
Hold the mnemonic slice: Sketch, then Limits and roots, then Choose the variable d x or d y, then Evaluate with absolute values and symmetry. Slice the region right and the integral writes itself.
चलो पहले subtopic को उन traps के साथ बंद करें जो marks खोते हैं और वो reflex जो उन्हें रोकता है।

number-one trap है negative या zero area report करना। जब भी curve axis के नीचे झुके raw integral negative हो जाता है, और अगर यह axis cross करे pieces cancel हो जाते हैं। हमेशा पहले sketch करो और f की absolute value का integral use करो, हर root पर split करते हुए।
दूसरा, गलत variable के respect में integrate करना। y-axis और horizontal lines से walled region को integral of x d y चाहिए, y d x नहीं। वहाँ d x force करना needless casework बनाता है।

तीसरा, limits invent करना। limits boundary lines हैं या वो points जहाँ curve axis से मिलता है — arbitrary numbers नहीं। four minus x squared जैसे curve के लिए, x-axis से bounded, limits हैं roots x equals plus और minus two, जिन्हें तुम्हें solve करना होगा।
चौथा, symmetry use करने के बाद वापस multiply करना भूल जाना। circle की first-quadrant area निकालकर times-four गिरा देना सिर्फ़ answer का एक चौथाई देता है।
पाँचवाँ, ellipse formula बिगाड़ना। यह है pi a b, semi-axes का product — pi a squared b squared नहीं, और pi times a plus b नहीं।

<curious> वो pro-tip जो तीनों सबसे बड़े mark-losers को मार देती है: integral छूने से पहले, पाँच सेकंड लो curve sketch करने और region shade करने के लिए, mark करो कहाँ यह axis cross करता है ताकि तुम split plan कर सको, और symmetry check करो ताकि तुम सबसे छोटा piece integrate करो।
mnemonic slice पकड़ो: Sketch, फिर Limits और roots, फिर Choose the variable d x या d y, फिर Evaluate absolute values और symmetry के साथ। region को सही slice करो और integral खुद लिख जाता है।

board_events.text: Subtopic 1 is just this with the bottom curve being the axis, $g(x) = 0$.
Wrinkle 1: the limits are the INTERSECTIONS — solve $f(x) = g(x)$.
Wrinkle 2: identify which curve is on top by testing a sample point between them.
If the curves swap on the interval, split at each crossing.

segments.text: In the first subtopic you found the area between a single curve and an axis. But the axis is really nothing special — it is just the flat line y equals zero. What if the floor of your region is itself a curve? Then you are looking at the area sandwiched between two curves, and your existing idea generalises in one clean stroke.

Picture the strip of land between two railway tracks running across a hilly stretch of the Konkan coast. The upper track follows one curve, the lower track another. Slice that strip into paper-thin vertical pieces, exactly as before.

Now each thin strip runs from the lower track up to the upper track, so its height is not the curve but the gap between the curves: top minus bottom, f of x minus g of x. Its width is still d x, so its area is the gap times d x.
Adding all the strips from where the tracks meet at x equals a to where they meet at x equals b gives the area: the integral from a to b of f of x minus g of x d x, valid when f is above g.
And notice — the single-curve case of the first subtopic is just this formula with the bottom curve being the x-axis, g of x equals zero. Nothing new to memorise, only a generalisation.

<curious> But two genuinely new wrinkles appear. First: where do the strips start and stop? The limits a and b are usually not handed to you — they are the points of intersection, the places where the strip-height shrinks to zero. You find them by solving f of x equals g of x.
Second: which curve is on top? Top minus bottom only works if you know which is which, so test one sample x between the intersection points. Guessing is the number-one source of sign errors here.

And the two curves may swap roles — f above g on one stretch, below it on another. Wherever they cross, the gap flips sign, so you must split the region at each crossing and always subtract the genuine lower curve from the genuine upper one.

पहले subtopic में तुमने एक single curve और एक axis के बीच की area निकाली। पर axis असल में कोई ख़ास चीज़ नहीं — यह बस flat line y equals zero है। अगर तुम्हारे region का floor खुद एक curve हो तो? तब तुम दो curves के बीच sandwiched area देख रहे हो, और तुम्हारा मौजूदा idea एक clean stroke में generalise हो जाता है।

Konkan coast के एक hilly stretch पर चलती दो railway tracks के बीच की ज़मीन की पट्टी सोचो। upper track एक curve follow करती है, lower track दूसरी। उस पट्टी को paper-thin vertical pieces में slice करो, बिलकुल पहले जैसे।

अब हर thin strip lower track से upper track तक जाती है, तो उसकी height curve नहीं बल्कि curves के बीच का gap है: top minus bottom, f of x minus g of x। इसकी width अभी भी d x है, तो इसकी area है gap times d x।
सारी strips को tracks के x equals a पर मिलने से x equals b पर मिलने तक add करने पर area मिलती है: integral from a to b of f of x minus g of x d x, valid जब f, g के ऊपर हो।
और ध्यान दो — पहले subtopic का single-curve case बस यही formula है जिसमें bottom curve x-axis है, g of x equals zero। कुछ नया memorise नहीं करना, सिर्फ़ एक generalisation।

<curious> पर दो सच में नए wrinkles आते हैं। पहला: strips कहाँ शुरू और खत्म होती हैं? limits a और b आमतौर पर तुम्हें नहीं दिए जाते — ये points of intersection हैं, वो जगहें जहाँ strip-height zero तक सिकुड़ जाती है। तुम इन्हें f of x equals g of x solve करके पाते हो।
दूसरा: कौन सा curve ऊपर है? top minus bottom तभी काम करता है जब तुम्हें पता हो कौन कौन है, तो intersection points के बीच एक sample x test करो। यहाँ guessing sign errors का number-one source है।

और दोनों curves roles swap कर सकते हैं — एक stretch पर f, g के ऊपर, दूसरे पर नीचे। जहाँ भी वे cross करें, gap sign flip करता है, तो तुम्हें हर crossing पर region split करना होगा और हमेशा genuine lower curve को genuine upper से subtract करना होगा।

sections.title: The between-curves theorem and the two-parabolas result

board_events.text: Why the formula holds even below the axis, and a catalogue result
Strip height is $f - g$; sum and pass to the limit (the Riemann argument).
If $g$ dips below the axis, shift everything up by $C$ — the gap is unchanged.
For $y^2 = 4ax$ and $x^2 = 4ay$: intersect at $(0,0)$ and $(4a, 4a)$.
The answer scales as $a^2$ — exactly as an area must.

segments.text: Let's prove the between-curves formula and derive one catalogue result. The proof is the same strip argument as before.

Take an elementary vertical strip. Its top edge sits on f of x and its bottom edge on g of x, so its height is f minus g and its area is f minus g times d x. Sum over all strips and pass to the limit — the same Riemann argument as the first subtopic.

<curious> But here is the subtle part: why does this hold even when a curve dips below the axis? Suppose g goes negative somewhere. Shift the entire picture up by a constant C large enough that both curves rise above the axis. Shifting does not change the gap between them, hence not the area.

And the algebra confirms it: the integral of f plus C minus g plus C equals the integral of f minus g — the constant simply cancels. So the formula is valid whether the curves lie above or below the axis, provided only that f is above g. That single proviso is the whole game.

Now the catalogue result — the area between the two parabolas y squared equals four a x and x squared equals four a y. Substituting one into the other, they intersect at the origin and at the point four a, four a.

Between those limits the upper branch is y equals two root a x and the lower is x squared over four a. Integrating top minus bottom gives thirty-two a squared over three, minus sixteen a squared over three.
That leaves sixteen a squared over three — the standard result for two equal parabolas.
And a quick check: the answer scales as a squared, exactly as any area must. A formula with the wrong dimensions is wrong on sight.
चलो between-curves formula prove करें और एक catalogue result derive करें। proof वही strip argument है जो पहले था।

एक elementary vertical strip लो। इसका top edge f of x पर बैठता है और bottom edge g of x पर, तो इसकी height f minus g है और area f minus g times d x। सारी strips पर sum करो और limit तक जाओ — पहले subtopic वाला ही Riemann argument।

<curious> पर यह रहा subtle हिस्सा: यह तब भी क्यों hold करता है जब कोई curve axis के नीचे झुके? मान लो g कहीं negative हो जाता है। पूरी picture को एक constant C से इतना ऊपर shift करो कि दोनों curves axis के ऊपर उठ जाएँ। shifting उनके बीच का gap नहीं बदलती, इसलिए area भी नहीं।

और algebra इसे confirm करता है: integral of f plus C minus g plus C equals integral of f minus g — constant बस cancel हो जाता है। तो formula valid है चाहे curves axis के ऊपर हों या नीचे, बशर्ते सिर्फ़ f, g के ऊपर हो। वो एक proviso ही पूरा खेल है।

अब catalogue result — दो parabolas y squared equals four a x और x squared equals four a y के बीच की area। एक को दूसरे में substitute करने पर, वे origin पर और point four a, four a पर intersect करती हैं।

उन limits के बीच upper branch है y equals two root a x और lower है x squared over four a। top minus bottom integrate करने पर मिलता है thirty-two a squared over three, minus sixteen a squared over three।
इससे बचता है sixteen a squared over three — दो equal parabolas का standard result।
और एक quick check: answer a squared के हिसाब से scale करता है, बिलकुल जैसे किसी भी area को करना चाहिए। गलत dimensions वाला formula देखते ही गलत है।

sections.title: The between-curves formula set

board_events.text: Vertical strips, horizontal strips, crossings, and a catalogue result
Limits = intersection points: solve $f(x) = g(x)$ (or $p(y) = q(y)$) FIRST.
Sideways-opening curves are far cleaner in $y$ (right − left) than forced into $dx$.

segments.text: Let's consolidate the between-curves toolkit. It is really one formula in four dresses.
With vertical strips, when f is above g, the area is the integral from a to b of top minus bottom, f minus g.
With horizontal strips, when p is to the right of q, the area is the integral from c to d of right minus left, p minus q.
When the curves cross inside the interval, the honest area is the integral of the absolute value of f minus g — you split at each crossing and add the magnitudes.
The special case ties it back to the first subtopic: set the lower curve to zero and you recover the plain area under a single curve.
And the catalogue result: the two parabolas y squared equals four a x and x squared equals four a y enclose sixteen a squared over three.

<whisper> The habit that saves you: the limits are the intersection points, found by solving f of x equals g of x first — never numbers copied from the question text. Skipping this step is the most common zero-out-of-five on boards.

And one strategic choice: sideways-opening curves, like a parabola written as x in terms of y, are far cleaner integrated in y as right minus left, rather than forced into d x with its awkward two-branch casework.
चलो between-curves toolkit consolidate करें। यह असल में चार पोशाकों में एक ही formula है।
vertical strips के साथ, जब f, g के ऊपर हो, area है integral from a to b of top minus bottom, f minus g।
horizontal strips के साथ, जब p, q के दाईं ओर हो, area है integral from c to d of right minus left, p minus q।
जब curves interval के अंदर cross करें, honest area है f minus g की absolute value का integral — तुम हर crossing पर split करते हो और magnitudes जोड़ते हो।
special case इसे पहले subtopic से वापस जोड़ता है: lower curve को zero रखो और तुम एक single curve के नीचे की plain area recover कर लेते हो।
और catalogue result: दो parabolas y squared equals four a x और x squared equals four a y घेरती हैं sixteen a squared over three।

<whisper> वो habit जो तुम्हें बचाती है: limits intersection points हैं, पहले f of x equals g of x solve करके पाए गए — कभी question text से copy किए numbers नहीं। यह step skip करना boards पर सबसे common zero-out-of-five है।

और एक strategic choice: sideways-opening curves, जैसे x को y के terms में लिखा parabola, y में right minus left के रूप में integrate करने पर कहीं cleaner हैं, बजाय d x में force करने के जिसमें awkward two-branch casework होता है।

segments.text: Let's start the between-curves examples with the cleanest pairing — the line y equals x and the parabola y equals x squared.
The picture shows a small lens-shaped region trapped between the two curves near the origin.
First, find the limits by intersecting. Setting x equals x squared gives x times x minus one equals zero, so the curves meet at x equals zero and x equals one. Those are our limits.
Now fix top versus bottom by testing a sample point. At x equals one half, the line gives zero point five while the parabola gives zero point two five — so the line y equals x is on top.
So the area is the integral from zero to one of the line minus the parabola, x minus x squared. Antidifferentiating gives x squared over two minus x cubed over three.
Evaluating from zero to one, that is one half minus one third, which is one sixth.

<curious> Notice the rhythm we followed: Intersect to get the limits, Sketch the region, Sample a point to fix top versus bottom, then Integrate. Do those four beats in order and the sign errors simply cannot happen.
चलो between-curves examples को सबसे clean pairing से शुरू करें — line y equals x और parabola y equals x squared।
picture origin के पास दोनों curves के बीच फँसा एक छोटा lens-shaped region दिखाता है।
पहले, intersect करके limits पाओ। x equals x squared रखने पर मिलता है x times x minus one equals zero, तो curves x equals zero और x equals one पर मिलती हैं। ये हमारे limits हैं।
अब एक sample point test करके top versus bottom fix करो। x equals one half पर, line देती है zero point five जबकि parabola देती है zero point two five — तो line y equals x ऊपर है।
तो area है integral from zero to one of line minus parabola, x minus x squared। antidifferentiate करने पर मिलता है x squared over two minus x cubed over three।
zero से one तक evaluate करने पर, यह one half minus one third है, यानी one sixth।

<curious> जो rhythm हमने follow किया उस पर ध्यान दो: limits पाने के लिए Intersect, region Sketch, top versus bottom fix करने के लिए एक point Sample, फिर Integrate। इन चार beats को order में करो और sign errors हो ही नहीं सकते।

sections.title: The swap trap: split at the crossing

board_events.text: Area enclosed between y = x and y = x³ for −1 ≤ x ≤ 1
The trap: $\int_{-1}^{1}(x - x^3)\,dx = 0$ (odd integrand) — but the region has area!
The curves cross at $x = -1, 0, 1$ and swap which is on top at $x = 0$.
On $(0,1)$: $x > x^3$, line on top. On $(-1,0)$: $x^3 > x$, cubic on top.
The instant two curves cross inside the interval — split, never integrate through.

segments.text: This is the between-curves version of the sign trap, and it catches even careful students. We want the area enclosed between y equals x and y equals x cubed for x from minus one to one.

<whisper> Here is the trap. The hasty move is the integral from minus one to one of x minus x cubed, which equals zero because the integrand is odd. But the region clearly has area — the trap has swallowed a real shape.
The reason is that the two curves cross at three points — minus one, zero, and one — and they swap which one is on top right at the origin.

Test the halves. On the interval from zero to one, x is greater than x cubed, so the line is on top. On the interval from minus one to zero, x cubed is greater than x, so the cubic is on top. The roles genuinely flip.
By symmetry the two halves have equal area, so the total is twice the integral from zero to one of x minus x cubed. Antidifferentiating gives x squared over two minus x to the fourth over four.
Evaluating, that is twice the quantity one half minus one quarter, which is one half.
So the true area is one half square unit. Burn in the rule: the instant two curves cross inside your interval, split — never integrate straight through a crossing.
यह between-curves वाला sign trap है, और यह careful students को भी पकड़ता है। हमें y equals x और y equals x cubed के बीच घिरी area चाहिए, x equals minus one से one तक।
<whisper> यह रहा trap। जल्दबाज़ move है integral from minus one to one of x minus x cubed, जो zero के बराबर है क्योंकि integrand odd है। पर region में साफ़ area है — trap ने एक असली shape निगल ली है।
वजह यह है कि दोनों curves तीन points पर cross करती हैं — minus one, zero, और one — और वे ठीक origin पर swap कर देती हैं कि कौन ऊपर है।
halves test करो। zero से one interval पर, x, x cubed से बड़ा है, तो line ऊपर है। minus one से zero interval पर, x cubed, x से बड़ा है, तो cubic ऊपर है। roles सच में flip करते हैं।
symmetry से दोनों halves की area बराबर है, तो total है twice the integral from zero to one of x minus x cubed। antidifferentiate करने पर मिलता है x squared over two minus x to the fourth over four।
evaluate करने पर, यह twice the quantity one half minus one quarter है, यानी one half।
तो true area है one half square unit। rule दिमाग में बिठा लो: जैसे ही दो curves तुम्हारे interval के अंदर cross करें, split करो — कभी किसी crossing के across सीधे integrate मत करो।

segments.text: This example shows the payoff of choosing your variable wisely. We want the area bounded by the parabola y squared equals four x and the line y equals two x minus four.
The picture already hints at the strategy — the parabola opens sideways, so horizontal strips, right curve minus left curve, will be far cleaner.
Write both curves as functions of y. The parabola becomes x equals y squared over four, and the line becomes x equals y plus four over two.
Intersect them: y squared over four equals y plus four over two gives y squared minus two y minus eight equals zero, which factors to y equals minus two and y equals four. Those are our y-limits.
Now fix right versus left. At y equals zero, the line gives x equals two while the parabola gives x equals zero — so the line is the right curve.
So the area is the integral from minus two to four of the line minus the parabola. Working the two pieces, the line part integrates to fifteen and the parabola part to six.
Subtracting gives nine. So the area is nine square units.

<curious> And here is why the choice mattered: had we used vertical strips, the parabola's two branches would have forced an awkward two-part integral. Choosing d y collapsed the whole thing into a single clean integral.
यह example variable को समझदारी से चुनने का payoff दिखाता है। हमें parabola y squared equals four x और line y equals two x minus four से bounded area चाहिए।
picture पहले ही strategy का इशारा देता है — parabola sideways खुलता है, तो horizontal strips, right curve minus left curve, कहीं cleaner होंगी।
दोनों curves को y के functions के रूप में लिखो। parabola बनता है x equals y squared over four, और line बनती है x equals y plus four over two।

इन्हें intersect करो: y squared over four equals y plus four over two देता है y squared minus two y minus eight equals zero, जो factor होता है y equals minus two और y equals four में। ये हमारे y-limits हैं।
अब right versus left fix करो। y equals zero पर, line देती है x equals two जबकि parabola देती है x equals zero — तो line right curve है।
तो area है integral from minus two to four of line minus parabola। दोनों pieces करने पर, line part integrate होकर fifteen बनता है और parabola part six।
subtract करने पर नौ मिलता है। तो area है nine square units।

<curious> और यह रही वजह कि choice क्यों matter करता था: अगर हम vertical strips use करते, parabola की दो branches एक awkward two-part integral force कर देतीं। d y चुनने ने पूरी चीज़ को एक single clean integral में collapse कर दिया।

segments.text: We finish the between-curves examples with a J E E Advanced classic — the region common to the interior of the parabola y squared equals four x and the interior of the circle x squared plus y squared equals five.
The picture reveals the key feature: the region's ceiling is not one curve but two. The parabola caps it near the origin, then the circle takes over further out.

First, the intersections. Substitute y squared equals four x into the circle to get x squared plus four x equals five, so x squared plus four x minus five equals zero, factoring to x equals one — we reject minus five since the parabola needs x non-negative.
So the curves meet at one comma two and one comma minus two. The region is symmetric about the x-axis, so we take the upper half and double.

<curious> Now the composite ceiling. Moving left to right, from x equals zero to x equals one the binding ceiling is the parabola, y equals two root x, because it is the lower of the two there. From x equals one to x equals root five, the binding ceiling is the circle, y equals root five minus x squared. So we split the integral at x equals one.

The first piece, the integral of two root x from zero to one, is four thirds. The second piece, using the catalogue antiderivative with a squared equals five, works out to five pi over four, minus one, minus five halves inverse sine of one over root five.
Combining and doubling gives two thirds, plus five pi over two, minus five inverse sine of one over root five — about six point two zero square units.

And the sanity check holds: the whole disc has area five pi, roughly fifteen point seven, and the common region taking under half of it is geometrically sensible. The composite split was the whole skill here.
हम between-curves examples को एक J E E Advanced classic से खत्म करते हैं — parabola y squared equals four x के interior और circle x squared plus y squared equals five के interior का common region।
picture key feature दिखाता है: region की ceiling एक नहीं बल्कि दो curves हैं। parabola इसे origin के पास cap करता है, फिर circle आगे जाकर संभाल लेता है।

पहले, intersections। y squared equals four x को circle में substitute करके मिलता है x squared plus four x equals five, तो x squared plus four x minus five equals zero, factor होकर x equals one — हम minus five reject करते हैं क्योंकि parabola को x non-negative चाहिए।
तो curves one comma two और one comma minus two पर मिलती हैं। region x-axis के बारे में symmetric है, तो हम upper half लेते हैं और double करते हैं।

<curious> अब composite ceiling। left से right चलते हुए, x equals zero से x equals one तक binding ceiling parabola है, y equals two root x, क्योंकि वहाँ यह दोनों में से नीचे वाला है। x equals one से x equals root five तक, binding ceiling circle है, y equals root five minus x squared। तो हम integral को x equals one पर split करते हैं।

पहला piece, zero से one तक two root x का integral, four thirds है। दूसरा piece, catalogue antiderivative को a squared equals five के साथ use करके, निकलता है five pi over four, minus one, minus five halves inverse sine of one over root five।
combine करके double करने पर मिलता है two thirds, plus five pi over two, minus five inverse sine of one over root five — करीब six point two zero square units।
और sanity check hold करता है: पूरे disc की area five pi है, करीब fifteen point seven, और common region जो उसका आधे से कम लेता है, geometrically sensible है। composite split ही यहाँ पूरी skill थी।

sections.title: Area between curves: the ISSI routine

board_events.text: Subtopic 2 — the traps, and the four-beat routine
AOI-TOP-BOTTOM: bottom − top flips the sign — confirm which curve is higher with a sample point.
AOI-LIMIT-INTERSECT: limits are intersection points — solve $f(x) = g(x)$, don't copy numbers.
AOI-CROSS-SPLIT: if the curves swap inside the interval, integrate $|f - g|$, splitting at the crossing.
AOI-AXIS-VAR: sideways curves and left/right-capped regions are cleaner in $y$ (right − left).
Verify symmetry before halving the work — false symmetry costs marks.
Pro-tip: pick the variable by the boundaries — curves on the sides → $dy$; curves on top/bottom → $dx$.
Mnemonic ISSI: Intersect → Sketch → Sample (which is on top) → Integrate top − bottom.

segments.text: Let's close the second subtopic with its traps and the routine that beats them.
The first trap is subtracting in the wrong order. Writing bottom minus top flips the sign and yields a negative area. Always confirm which curve is higher by plugging in one sample x.

Second, inventing the limits. The limits are the intersection points, found by solving f of x equals g of x — not numbers copied from the question text. Skipping this is the most common zero-out-of-five on boards.
Third, integrating across a swap. If the curves cross inside the interval, the top and bottom roles switch, so integrate the absolute value of f minus g, splitting at each crossing.

Fourth, fighting the geometry with the wrong variable. Sideways-opening parabolas and regions capped left and right are far cleaner in y, as right minus left. Forcing d x creates needless two-branch casework.
And fifth, assuming false symmetry. Doubling a half-area only works if the region is truly symmetric about that axis — verify before you halve the work.

<curious> The pro-tip that decides everything quickly: pick the variable by the boundaries. If the region's sides are the curves and its top and bottom are horizontal, use d y. If its top and bottom are the curves and its sides are vertical, use d x. Match the strip to the geometry.

Hold the mnemonic I S S I: Intersect for the limits, Sketch both curves, Sample one interior point to fix top versus bottom and spot any swap, then Integrate top minus bottom. Always top minus bottom, every strip, every time.
चलो दूसरे subtopic को इसके traps और उन्हें हराने वाली routine के साथ बंद करें।
पहला trap है गलत order में subtract करना। bottom minus top लिखना sign flip कर देता है और एक negative area देता है। हमेशा एक sample x डालकर confirm करो कि कौन सा curve ऊँचा है।
दूसरा, limits invent करना। limits intersection points हैं, f of x equals g of x solve करके पाए गए — question text से copy किए numbers नहीं। यह skip करना boards पर सबसे common zero-out-of-five है।
तीसरा, एक swap के across integrate करना। अगर curves interval के अंदर cross करें, top और bottom roles switch हो जाते हैं, तो f minus g की absolute value integrate करो, हर crossing पर split करते हुए।

चौथा, गलत variable से geometry से लड़ना। sideways-opening parabolas और left-right capped regions y में कहीं cleaner हैं, right minus left के रूप में। d x force करना needless two-branch casework बनाता है।
और पाँचवाँ, false symmetry मान लेना। एक half-area को double करना तभी काम करता है जब region सच में उस axis के बारे में symmetric हो — काम आधा करने से पहले verify करो।

<curious> वो pro-tip जो सब कुछ जल्दी decide करती है: variable को boundaries से चुनो। अगर region के sides curves हों और top-bottom horizontal, तो d y use करो। अगर top-bottom curves हों और sides vertical, तो d x। strip को geometry से match करो।

mnemonic I S S I पकड़ो: limits के लिए Intersect, दोनों curves Sketch, top versus bottom fix करने और कोई swap spot करने के लिए एक interior point Sample, फिर top minus bottom Integrate। हमेशा top minus bottom, हर strip, हर बार।

board_events.text: Disguise 1 — modulus: $y = |x|$ is a 'V' with a corner; split at every corner.
Disguise 2 — inequality: $y \le f(x)$ is a region (one side), not a curve.
A system like $\{y \ge x^2,\; y \le x + 2\}$ is the OVERLAP of two such regions.
Disguise 3 — composite: the ceiling is one curve, then switches to another.
Nothing new is integrated here — the skill is decoding the boundary.
The mistakes happen in the decoding, almost never in the calculus.

segments.text: By now you can find the area under one curve and between two curves. Here is the reassuring truth about the whole J E E layer of this chapter: every hard area problem is one of those two in disguise. The only extra work is stripping off the disguise, and three disguises appear again and again.
The board shows all three at a glance — a V-shaped modulus, an overlap of inequalities, and a switching skyline ceiling.

Disguise one is the modulus. A curve like y equals mod x has a corner. The modulus simply reflects whatever part of the inside is negative back up to positive, so mod x is a V: the line y equals x for x non-negative, and y equals minus x for x negative, joined at a kink at the origin. To handle it, split the interval at every corner and integrate each smooth piece — exactly the splitting you already do for a curve that crosses the axis.
Disguise two is the inequality. A condition like y less than or equal to f of x is not a curve at all; it is a region — everything on one side of the curve.

A system such as y greater than or equal to x squared, and y less than or equal to x plus two, is the overlap of two such regions. Your job is to translate each inequality into which side, sketch the overlap, and read off the upper and lower boundaries — after which it is a plain between-curves problem.

Disguise three is the composite region. Sometimes the ceiling is one curve for a while, then switches to a different curve. Picture a Mumbai skyline: one building, then a taller one, then a shorter one. Split the range at each point where the tallest boundary changes, integrate each slab, and add.
<curious> The unifying insight: every one of these is a decoding puzzle followed by routine integration. Nothing new is integrated here — decode the boundary, and the integral writes itself.
So the mistakes in this subtopic happen in the decoding — finding the corners, deciding the sides, locating the switch points — almost never in the calculus itself.

अब तक तुम एक curve के नीचे और दो curves के बीच की area निकाल सकते हो। इस chapter की पूरी J E E layer के बारे में यह भरोसा देने वाली सच्चाई है: हर hard area problem उन्हीं दो में से एक का disguise है। एकमात्र extra काम disguise उतारना है, और तीन disguises बार-बार आते हैं।
board तीनों को एक नज़र में दिखाता है — एक V-shaped modulus, inequalities का overlap, और एक switching skyline ceiling।

पहला disguise modulus है। y equals mod x जैसे curve का एक corner होता है। modulus बस inside के जो हिस्से negative हैं उन्हें वापस positive में reflect कर देता है, तो mod x एक V है: x non-negative के लिए line y equals x, और x negative के लिए y equals minus x, origin पर एक kink पर जुड़े हुए। इसे handle करने के लिए, हर corner पर interval split करो और हर smooth piece integrate करो — बिलकुल वो splitting जो तुम axis cross करते curve के लिए पहले से करते हो।
दूसरा disguise inequality है। y less than or equal to f of x जैसी condition बिलकुल curve नहीं; यह एक region है — curve के एक तरफ़ का सब कुछ।

y greater than or equal to x squared, और y less than or equal to x plus two, जैसा system दो ऐसे regions का overlap है। तुम्हारा काम है हर inequality को which side में translate करना, overlap sketch करना, और upper तथा lower boundaries पढ़ना — जिसके बाद यह एक plain between-curves problem है।

तीसरा disguise composite region है। कभी-कभी ceiling कुछ देर एक curve होती है, फिर एक अलग curve पर switch कर जाती है। एक Mumbai skyline सोचो: एक building, फिर एक ऊँची, फिर एक छोटी। range को हर उस point पर split करो जहाँ सबसे ऊँची boundary बदलती है, हर slab integrate करो, और जोड़ो।
<curious> unifying insight: इनमें से हर एक एक decoding puzzle है जिसके बाद routine integration आता है। यहाँ कुछ नया integrate नहीं होता — boundary decode करो, और integral खुद लिख जाता है।
तो इस subtopic में गलतियाँ decoding में होती हैं — corners ढूँढना, sides तय करना, switch points locate करना — लगभग कभी calculus में नहीं।

board_events.text: Three procedures, and the |x| + |y| ≤ a area
A — modulus: set each inside to zero for the corners, replace by $\pm f$, integrate each piece.
B — inequalities: decode each side, sketch the overlap, integrate top − bottom, test a point.
C — composite: solve the two boundaries equal to find the switch, split, sum the slabs.
Diamond theorem: $|x| + |y| \le a$ is symmetric in all four quadrants.

board_events.latex: \text{1st quadrant: } x + y \le a,\; x,y \ge 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \text{right triangle, legs } a

board_events.text: The same argument on $\tfrac{|x|}{p} + \tfrac{|y|}{q} \le 1$ gives $2pq$.

segments.text: Let's lay out the three decoding procedures, then prove the one catalogue result of this subtopic.

Procedure A, for a modulus or piecewise curve: set the inside of each modulus to zero to locate the corners, then on each sub-interval replace the modulus by plus f or minus f according to its sign, integrate each piece, and add — using symmetry to shorten the work if the picture is symmetric.

Procedure B, for a region from inequalities: decode each inequality into which side, sketch the boundary curves and shade the overlap, find the intersection points for your limits, and integrate top minus bottom — always testing a point to confirm you shaded the correct side.

Procedure C, for a composite region: find where the boundary switches by solving the two candidate boundaries equal to each other, split the range at each switch point, and on each slab use the boundary that is actually extreme there, then sum the slabs.

Now the diamond theorem. The region mod x plus mod y less than or equal to a is symmetric in all four quadrants, because replacing x by minus x or y by minus y leaves the condition unchanged. So its area is four times the first-quadrant part.
In the first quadrant, mod x is x and mod y is y, so the condition becomes x plus y less than or equal to a with x and y non-negative — a right triangle with both legs of length a.
<excited> So the total area is four times one half a times a, which is two a squared. Short, clean, and worth memorising outright.
And the very same argument on mod x over p plus mod y over q less than or equal to one gives a first-quadrant triangle with legs p and q, hence total area two p q.
चलो तीन decoding procedures रखें, फिर इस subtopic का एकमात्र catalogue result prove करें।

Procedure A, एक modulus या piecewise curve के लिए: corners locate करने के लिए हर modulus के inside को zero रखो, फिर हर sub-interval पर modulus को उसके sign के हिसाब से plus f या minus f से replace करो, हर piece integrate करो, और जोड़ो — अगर picture symmetric हो तो symmetry से काम छोटा करो।

Procedure B, inequalities से region के लिए: हर inequality को which side में decode करो, boundary curves sketch करके overlap shade करो, अपने limits के लिए intersection points ढूँढो, और top minus bottom integrate करो — हमेशा एक point test करके confirm करो कि तुमने सही side shade की।

Procedure C, composite region के लिए: दोनों candidate boundaries को एक-दूसरे के बराबर solve करके पता करो boundary कहाँ switch होती है, हर switch point पर range split करो, और हर slab पर वो boundary use करो जो वहाँ सच में extreme है, फिर slabs जोड़ो।

अब diamond theorem। region mod x plus mod y less than or equal to a चारों quadrants में symmetric है, क्योंकि x को minus x या y को minus y से replace करना condition नहीं बदलता। तो इसकी area first-quadrant part का four times है।
first quadrant में, mod x है x और mod y है y, तो condition बन जाती है x plus y less than or equal to a, x और y non-negative के साथ — एक right triangle जिसकी दोनों legs की length a है।
<excited> तो total area है four times one half a times a, यानी two a squared। छोटा, clean, और सीधे memorise करने लायक।
और वही argument mod x over p plus mod y over q less than or equal to one पर एक first-quadrant triangle देता है legs p और q के साथ, इसलिए total area two p q।

board_events.text: The decoding toolkit for advanced regions

board_events.latex: |f(x)| = \begin{cases} f(x), & f(x) \ge 0 \\ -f(x), & f(x) < 0 \end{cases} \;\; \text{— split at the roots of } f

board_events.text: $y \le f$ = below; $y \ge f$ = above; $x^2+y^2 \le r^2$ = inside; $y \ge |x|$ = above the V.
For a system, the region is the INTERSECTION of these — confirm with a test point.
Symmetry: $y$-axis → 2× right half; $x$-axis → 2× upper half; four-fold → 4× first quadrant.
Decode first, integrate second — verify every corner, side, and switch point.

segments.text: Let's consolidate the decoding toolkit for advanced regions. None of it changes the integration — it only tells you what to integrate.

First, the modulus expansion: mod f equals f where f is non-negative, and minus f where f is negative. The practical instruction is to split the domain at the roots of f, exactly where the sign flips.
Second, the diamond results: mod x over p plus mod y over q at most one encloses area two p q, and the classic mod x plus mod y at most a encloses two a squared.

Third, the inequality decode: y less than or equal to f is below the curve, y greater than or equal to f is above it, x squared plus y squared at most r squared is inside the circle, and y greater than or equal to mod x is the wedge above the V.
For a system of inequalities, the region is the intersection of all of them — and you should always confirm which side you shaded with an easy test point, often the origin.
For a composite region where the ceiling switches at x equals s, split the integral there: top-one minus bottom up to the switch, then top-two minus bottom beyond it.

<curious> And the symmetry catalogue saves real time: symmetry about the y-axis means twice the right half, about the x-axis twice the upper half, and four-fold symmetry — like the diamond — means four times the first-quadrant piece.
The governing principle throughout: decode first, integrate second. Verify every corner, every side, and every switch point before you write a single integral.
चलो advanced regions के लिए decoding toolkit consolidate करें। इसमें से कुछ भी integration नहीं बदलता — यह सिर्फ़ बताता है कि क्या integrate करना है।
पहले, modulus expansion: mod f equals f जहाँ f non-negative है, और minus f जहाँ f negative है। practical instruction है domain को f के roots पर split करना, ठीक वहाँ जहाँ sign flip होता है।
दूसरा, diamond results: mod x over p plus mod y over q ज़्यादा से ज़्यादा one area two p q घेरता है, और classic mod x plus mod y ज़्यादा से ज़्यादा a घेरता है two a squared।

तीसरा, inequality decode: y less than or equal to f curve के नीचे है, y greater than or equal to f इसके ऊपर, x squared plus y squared ज़्यादा से ज़्यादा r squared circle के अंदर, और y greater than or equal to mod x वो wedge है जो V के ऊपर है।
inequalities के एक system के लिए, region उन सबका intersection है — और तुम्हें हमेशा एक easy test point से, अक्सर origin से, confirm करना चाहिए कि कौन सी side shade की।
एक composite region के लिए जहाँ ceiling x equals s पर switch करती है, integral वहाँ split करो: switch तक top-one minus bottom, फिर उसके आगे top-two minus bottom।

<curious> और symmetry catalogue असली time बचाता है: y-axis के बारे में symmetry का मतलब right half का दुगना, x-axis के बारे में upper half का दुगना, और four-fold symmetry — diamond जैसी — का मतलब first-quadrant piece का चार गुना।
पूरे समय governing principle: पहले decode, दूसरे integrate। एक भी integral लिखने से पहले हर corner, हर side, और हर switch point verify करो।

board_events.text: A modulus always contributes a corner — split there, exactly like a sign change.

segments.text: Let's start the advanced examples with the simplest disguise — a modulus. We want the area bounded by y equals mod x, the x-axis, and the lines x equals minus two and x equals three.
The picture shows the V with its corner at the origin. That corner is where the inside of the modulus changes sign, so we split the interval there.
On the left piece, from minus two to zero, mod x is minus x. On the right piece, from zero to three, mod x is just x.
So the area is the integral from minus two to zero of minus x, plus the integral from zero to three of x.
The left piece antidifferentiates to minus x squared over two, giving zero minus minus two, which is two. The right piece gives nine over two.
Adding them, two plus nine over two is thirteen over two. So the area is thirteen over two square units.
The takeaway: a modulus always contributes a corner, and you split there — it is exactly the same splitting reflex you use when a curve changes sign.
चलो advanced examples को सबसे simple disguise से शुरू करें — एक modulus। हमें y equals mod x, x-axis, और lines x equals minus two और x equals three से bounded area चाहिए।
picture V को origin पर उसके corner के साथ दिखाता है। वो corner वहाँ है जहाँ modulus का inside sign बदलता है, तो हम interval वहाँ split करते हैं।
left piece पर, minus two से zero तक, mod x है minus x। right piece पर, zero से three तक, mod x बस x है।
तो area है integral from minus two to zero of minus x, plus integral from zero to three of x।
left piece antidifferentiate होकर minus x squared over two बनता है, देता है zero minus minus two, यानी two। right piece देता है nine over two।
इन्हें add करने पर, two plus nine over two है thirteen over two। तो area है thirteen over two square units।
takeaway: एक modulus हमेशा एक corner देता है, और तुम वहाँ split करते हो — यह वही splitting reflex है जो तुम curve के sign बदलने पर use करते हो।

board_events.text: The trap: keeping the moduli inside one messy integral, or miscounting 'side squared'.

segments.text: This example rewards recognising a shape instead of grinding. We want the area of the region mod x plus mod y less than or equal to two.
The picture reveals it: a tilted square — a diamond — with vertices at plus and minus two on the x-axis and plus and minus two on the y-axis.
<whisper> Here is the trap. Students either try to set up a single messy integral with the moduli still inside, or they recognise it as a square but miscount the area as side squared. Both go wrong.
The clean way is simply the diamond theorem with a equals two.
So the area is two a squared, which is two times two squared, equal to eight.

And a completely independent check confirms it: the diagonals are each of length four, and a square's area is one half the product of its diagonals — one half times four times four, which is also eight.

<curious> Two independent routes landing on the same eight is exactly the reassurance you want. The lesson is to decode the boundary as a diamond and reach for the shape formula, rather than grinding through moduli inside an integral.
यह example grinding के बजाय एक shape पहचानने का इनाम देता है। हमें region mod x plus mod y less than or equal to two की area चाहिए।
picture इसे दिखाता है: एक tilted square — एक diamond — जिसके vertices x-axis पर plus और minus two, और y-axis पर plus और minus two हैं।

<whisper> यह रहा trap। students या तो moduli को अभी भी अंदर रखे हुए एक single messy integral set up करने की कोशिश करते हैं, या इसे square पहचानते हैं पर area को side squared के रूप में गलत गिनते हैं। दोनों गलत जाते हैं।
clean तरीका बस diamond theorem है a equals two के साथ।
तो area है two a squared, यानी two times two squared, बराबर eight।
और एक बिलकुल independent check इसे confirm करता है: diagonals हर एक length four की हैं, और एक square की area इसके diagonals के product की आधी है — one half times four times four, जो भी eight है।

<curious> दो independent routes का एक ही eight पर पहुँचना ठीक वो भरोसा है जो तुम चाहते हो। सबक है boundary को diamond के रूप में decode करना और shape formula reach करना, बजाय एक integral के अंदर moduli घिसने के।

board_events.text: Area of the region {y ≥ x², y ≤ x + 2}
Decode: $y \ge x^2$ is above the parabola; $y \le x+2$ is below the line — a lens.
Line on top, parabola on the bottom, between $x = -1$ and $x = 2$.
Decode each inequality into a side, then it collapses into a plain between-curves problem.

segments.text: This example is disguise two — a region defined by inequalities. We want the area of the set where y is at least x squared and at most x plus two.

Decode each condition into a side. y greater than or equal to x squared is the region above the parabola; y less than or equal to x plus two is the region below the line. Their overlap is a lens, with the line on top and the parabola on the bottom.
Find the limits by intersecting the boundaries: x squared equals x plus two gives x squared minus x minus two equals zero, which factors to x equals minus one and x equals two.
So the line is the ceiling and the parabola is the floor, between x equals minus one and x equals two.
The area is the integral from minus one to two of the line minus the parabola, x plus two minus x squared. Antidifferentiating gives x squared over two plus two x minus x cubed over three.

Evaluating: at x equals two we get ten thirds, and at x equals minus one we get minus seven sixths. Subtracting, ten thirds minus minus seven sixths is twenty sixths plus seven sixths, which is twenty-seven sixths.
That simplifies to nine over two square units.
The whole move was decoding: turn each inequality into a side, and the problem collapses into a plain between-curves calculation.
यह example disguise दो है — inequalities से परिभाषित एक region। हमें उस set की area चाहिए जहाँ y कम से कम x squared और ज़्यादा से ज़्यादा x plus two है।

हर condition को एक side में decode करो। y greater than or equal to x squared parabola के ऊपर का region है; y less than or equal to x plus two line के नीचे का region है। इनका overlap एक lens है, line ऊपर और parabola नीचे के साथ।
boundaries को intersect करके limits पाओ: x squared equals x plus two देता है x squared minus x minus two equals zero, जो factor होता है x equals minus one और x equals two में।
तो line ceiling है और parabola floor, x equals minus one और x equals two के बीच।
area है integral from minus one to two of line minus parabola, x plus two minus x squared। antidifferentiate करने पर मिलता है x squared over two plus two x minus x cubed over three।

evaluate करना: x equals two पर हमें ten thirds मिलता है, और x equals minus one पर minus seven sixths। subtract करने पर, ten thirds minus minus seven sixths है twenty sixths plus seven sixths, यानी twenty-seven sixths।
यह simplify होकर nine over two square units बनता है।
पूरा move decoding था: हर inequality को एक side में बदलो, और problem एक plain between-curves calculation में collapse हो जाता है।

segments.text: We finish the subtopic with an Advanced region that combines a modulus wedge and a circle — and a beautiful geometry check at the end. We want the area where y is at least mod x and x squared plus y squared is at most two.

Decode both. y greater than or equal to mod x is the wedge above both lines y equals x and y equals minus x; x squared plus y squared at most two is the inside of a circle of radius root two. The region is the slice of the disc sitting above the V.

Find the intersections: on y equals mod x, the circle gives x squared plus x squared equals two, so x squared equals one and x equals plus or minus one. The region is symmetric about the y-axis, so take the right half — from zero to one, bottom y equals x, top the circle — and double.
So the area is twice the integral from zero to one of root two minus x squared, minus x.

Using the catalogue antiderivative with a squared equals two, the integral of root two minus x squared from zero to one is one half plus pi over four. And the integral of x from zero to one is one half.

segments.text: Let's close the advanced subtopic with its traps and the one discipline that prevents them all.

The first trap is missing a corner of a modulus curve. Every modulus contributes a kink, so set each inside-expression to zero and split there. A nested modulus like mod, mod x minus one, has two corners — miss one and your limits are wrong.

Second, shading the wrong side of an inequality. Translate the less-than-or-equal and greater-than-or-equal carefully, and confirm with a test point — the origin is easiest whenever it is not on a boundary.
Third, forgetting to split a composite region. When the top boundary switches partway across, a single integral cannot cover both slabs — you must split at the switch point.
Fourth, assuming symmetry that isn't there, or forgetting to multiply back after using it. Symmetry is a gift only after you have verified it.

segments.text: Welcome to Application of Integrals. You already know the area of a rectangle, a triangle, or a circle from memorised formulas. But what is the area of a region trapped under a curvy boundary, like under the arch y equals x squared plus one? There is no clean formula — and integration is exactly what fills that gap.

Here is the picture to carry through the whole chapter. Imagine a land surveyor measuring an irregular farm plot. One edge runs along a straight canal — that's our x-axis — and the opposite edge is a wavy stream described by some curve y equals f of x.
The clever surveyor slices the plot into a long series of very thin vertical strips, each as narrow as a sheet of paper.
Each strip is almost a rectangle: its width is a tiny d x, and its height is the value of the curve at that spot, so one strip has area about y d x, which is f of x d x.

<curious> To get the whole plot, add up the areas of all these strips from the well at x equals a to the banyan tree at x equals b. Adding up infinitely many infinitely-thin strips is precisely what the definite integral means: the area is the integral from a to b of f of x d x.

Sometimes the boundary is measured more naturally against the vertical canal — the curve is given as x equals g of y. Then the same logic just flips axes, and you sweep horizontal strips up the y-axis.
In that case each strip is horizontal, with height d y and length x equals g of y, swept from y equals c to y equals d.

The one habit to install now: pick the variable that matches the geometry. If the region is walled left and right by vertical lines, d x strips win; if it's capped above and below by horizontal lines, d y strips are cleaner. Choose badly and a one-line integral becomes a messy two-piece one.
Let's make the strip picture rigorous — this is the theorem that justifies the whole method. Take f continuous and non-negative on the interval from a to b.
Partition that interval into n sub-intervals, each of width delta x equal to b minus a over n, with division points from x-nought up to x-n.
The width of each piece is delta x, and the division points march evenly across the interval.
Over the i-th sub-interval, pick any sample point xi-sub-i. The thin strip standing there is approximately a rectangle of height f of xi-sub-i and width delta x.
Summing all these rectangles gives an approximation to the area: S-n equals the sum over i of f of xi-sub-i times delta x.

<curious> Now here's why it becomes exact. The thinner the strips, the smaller the sliver of error between each rectangle and the true curved strip. As we let n go to infinity, so delta x shrinks to zero, those slivers vanish completely.
So the approximating sum converges to the exact area: the limit as n goes to infinity of that sum equals the integral from a to b of f of x d x.
And that final equality is not a coincidence — it is the very definition of the definite integral as a Riemann sum. The strip intuition and the integral are one and the same thing.
Now two results worth memorising — the areas of a circle and an ellipse — both proved the same clean way, using symmetry plus one standard antiderivative.

That antiderivative is the workhorse of the whole chapter: the integral of root a squared minus x squared is x over two times root a squared minus x squared, plus a squared over two times inverse sine of x over a, plus a constant.

For the circle x squared plus y squared equals a squared, exploit symmetry about both axes. The total area is four times the first-quadrant area, where the upper boundary is y equals root a squared minus x squared and x runs from zero to a.

<curious> Evaluating that standard integral from zero to a gives pi a squared over four, so four times it is exactly pi a squared. Integrating only the first quadrant removes any sign ambiguity and lets us evaluate the integral just once.
The ellipse follows immediately. Solving its equation for the upper half gives y equals b over a, times root a squared minus x squared.
By the same two-axis symmetry, the area is four b over a times the same integral from zero to a — which we already know is pi a squared over four — so the ellipse area is pi a b.

<whisper> And here is a beautiful self-check. Set b equal to a, and the ellipse collapses into a circle — and its area pi a b collapses correctly into pi a squared. A formula that degenerates correctly is almost certainly right.

The lesson under both proofs is symmetry: whenever a region is symmetric about an axis, compute the area of one symmetric part and simply multiply. It is the single biggest time-saver in this chapter.
